title: While Puerto Ricans protest for reliable access to water, the governor washes her hands
summary:
Leaky aqueducts and mega-projects for the wealthy exacerbate a water crisis in the US island territory

After more than a year without consistent service in San Juan, Puerto Rico , she fills them whenever water returns, which sometimes only happens for a handful of hours every few days. Going without reliable water to bathe, flush toilets or cook has affected her ability to work and stick to a usual routine – a catch-22, now that she has to spend more money and time buying water and prepared food. This summer, water levels in the island’s key dams fell below the thresholds needed to supply about half a million residents, leading to a severe drought that prompted Puerto Rico’s governor, Jenniffer González-Colón, to declare a state of emergency. But residents of San Juan, including Rivera, had already spent months grappling with water insecurity as the archipelago’s ageing and deteriorating infrastructure continued to fail amid government mismanagement. The water crisis has only amplified residents’ frustrations at the Puerto Rican government’s lack of solutions to protect the archipelago’s water. For example, the planned luxury development called Esencia is expected to consume more than a million gallons of water on the south-western tip of Puerto Rico, where residents have for years been grappling with intermittent service. Some local activists have also pointed out that the government could require residents to install rainwater catchment systems , which could provide millions of gallons of water a year. View image in fullscreen Dhara Rivera de Jesús always keeps a reserve of water for her family, a common household practice in Puerto Rico. “We recognize the drought, but we also recognize that there is an intellectual drought,” Rivera said. Even in safe-haven Massachusetts, trans care is at risk. Young people are fighting to protect it Read more Rivera and Alfredo Cuyar, residents of the San Juan neighborhood of Santurce, formed the Coalición Exigimos Agua (We Demand Water Coalition) in October. Their demands to the government were clear: residents want reliable water service. The coalition has since organized protests that have gathered thousands of Puerto Ricans on the archipelago, while diaspora communities in the continental US have followed, protesting in New York and Philadelphia against Esencia and the water crisis. “The level of frustration among citizens regarding essential services and social issues is growing,” Cuyar said. Other groups, including the feminist-focused Colectiva Feminista en Construcción, founded in 2014, have also joined the call for reliable water, alongside political groups such as the Movimiento Socialista de Trabajadores y Trabajadoras, La Jota and Se Acabaron Las Promesas. In August, several of these groups protested outside two hotel events hosted by González-Colón to celebrate her birthday and raise campaign funds. On Labor Day, dozens of people protested in San Juan to demand sweeping changes to the archipelago’s water infrastructure, as well as to the management of Puerto Rico’s Aqueduct and Sewer Authority (Prasa). Even Bad Bunny labeled the water crisis as a government attempt to sell “off the island piece by piece and fulfill their mission of a Puerto Rico without Puerto Ricans”.
